- NYMEX Henry Hub front-month prices have declined sharply: November 2026 contract fell from around $3.28 (mid-October) to about $2.60 by Oct 26; November contract settled at $2.82 on Oct 28. December was trading roughly $2.90–$3.07 intraday on Oct 29.

- Demand dynamics through Oct 29 show total gas demand up 4.7% year-over-year, driven by higher exports (up ~7.2%) and domestic use (up 3.5%), while residential/commercial demand rose sharply (+49.5% month-to-date) as heating kicks in and power-sector demand eased (down ~18.3% from September).
- Domestic gas production remains robust, over 4% above year-ago levels through Oct 29, supported by LNG demand and strong power-sector consumption. Major producers signal higher output in 2026 with capex near 2025 levels (Expand Energy guidance: ~7.45–7.55 Bcf/d for 2026, ~$3B capex).
- U.S. LNG exports hit a new high (~19.9 Bcf/d on Oct 1), reinforcing strong global demand despite softer domestic pricing.
- Net takeaway: Price outlook is skewed to softer near-term levels due to warm forecasts and robust supply, even as export demand remains resilient. If NOAA/El Niño patterns persist, domestic heating demand may remain tempered in the coming weeks, but episodic cold spells could provide episodic support.

news.title: Need to know: gas in Winter 2026-27  | Wood Mackenzie
news.summary:
Summary:

- Global gas market is tightening due to reduced LNG volumes from the Middle East (Qatar/UAE) and resulting competition for spot cargoes, pushing prices higher.
- Europe faces slow storage injections and high prices ahead of winter; TTF surpassed 100 €/MWh in late Oct. Fuel switching (gas-to-coal) has reduced European industrial gas demand by ~20% since 2022, with further reductions risking economic recession.
- Oil price and associated gas dynamics: Loss of Gulf and Russian oil reduces volumes, boosting US Lower 48 gas output and lowering Henry Hub prices, but rising oil production could increase associated gas and tighten pipelines by 2027.
- LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz are the key near-term uncertainty: normalisation would ease prices (reflecting lower oil prices and potentially more fuel switching in Asia); continued disruptions would keep global gas balances tight and prices elevated into 2027/28.
- European storage is expected to be about 75% full by end-October but end-winter storage could be around 17% of capacity under base case, with large regional disparities and upside price risk in a colder winter scenario.
- Market outlook: Europe to continue attracting marginal LNG cargoes through 2027 with higher-for-longer prices; any new disruptions could worsen tightness. If Hormuz flows normalise, oil price declines could lower gas competition in Asia, but persistent disruption could leave only minimal gas available for essential Asian demand and European storage replenishment.

news.title: Australian crop margins remain under pressure, but yields provide some relief

Higher yields in Victoria, South Australia, and above-average Western Australia production help spread costs over larger volumes, but abundant local supply may depress farmgate prices. Queensland and northern NSW face more exposure due to weaker rainfall and yield prospects.
- Farm-level responses: Some growers reduced fertiliser use and shifted from wheat to lower-input crops; some have pre-purchased fertiliser and increased on-farm diesel storage, raising working capital needs.
- Global outlook: Recovery in margins expected to be delayed and uneven. El Niño adds uncertainty into 2027. Fertiliser prices remain firm amid Middle East tensions; the US shows vulnerability with corn margins near breakeven or negative, while Europe and Brazil/A Argentina-margins show potential improvement.
- Overall: Limited scope for broad profitability improvements in 2027; margins will diverge by crop and region, with price gains constrained by ample world supplies and higher input costs.

news.title: World Bank Forecasts Higher Grain... | Syngenta CA
news.summary:
Summary:

- The World Bank’s Commodity Markets Outlook (Oct 2026) forecasts higher global grain and oilseed prices through 2027, driven by tightening supplies, adverse weather, strong biofuel demand, and Black Sea trade disruptions.
- Grain outlook:
  - Wheat: prices up 28% in 2026, then +14% in 2027, with an 11% drop anticipated in 2028. Global wheat production seen down 3% in 2026-27; large declines in US (-23%), Canada (-12%), Argentina (-23%), and Australia (-25%). Russia/Ukraine exports also set to fall due to ongoing hostilities.
  - Corn: prices up 10% in 2026 and 5% in 2027, due to a ~3% global production decline.
- Oilseeds:
  - Soybeans: prices up 18% in 2026 and 5% in 2027; soybean oil up 39% in 2026 and 11% in 2027; soybean meal up 18% and 10% over the same periods. Palm oil up 14% in 2026 and 10% in 2027. Global crops remain record or near-record, aiding some price support.
- Fertilizers: prices expected to rise ~14% in 2026, with urea-driven strength; potash also higher as farmers shift buys. Prices projected to normalize to 2025 levels by 2027 as energy costs ease and supply improves.
- Overall market note: Despite tighter grain supplies, total global grain availability for 2026-27 should still be the second-largest on record, which helps cap runaway price increases.
- Risks: Further El Niño intensification, ongoing Black Sea disruptions, and Middle East supply shocks could push prices higher than baseline forecasts.

Key takeaway for agricultural commodities traders: expect continued upward pressure on grains (notably wheat) and oilseeds through 2027, with fertilizer costs adding input-side support, while supply resilience remains a moderating factor unless geopolitical or climate risks intensify. news.title: What’s Behind the Latest Surge in Grain and Oilseed Prices? | Institutional Investor
news.summary:
Key takeaways on the agricultural commodities market outlook:

- Prices for grains and oilseeds have surged due to multiple shocks: geopolitical conflicts, adverse weather in key growing regions, and tighter-than-expected supply forecasts. The pullback in old-crop inventories and exogenous market shocks amplify late-summer/early-fall moves.
- CME Group Agriculture Index shows broad strength, with corn and oats up more than 12% since early August (through mid-September). Wheat, rough rice, soybeans, and soybean meal are up 8%+ in continuous futures.
- Energy costs and input pressures: higher energy costs have driven regional agricultural diesel prices up over 40%, contributing to broader cost pressures in farming and logistics. Exports remain steady at ~20% of annual production, supported by strong domestic ethanol demand.
- Crop fundamentals and WASDE catalysts:
  - Corn: USDA's August WASDE trimmed yields and ending stocks below expectations; September WASDE reiterated lower yields (178.5 bushels/acre) and tightened ending stocks, fueling continued rally above $5/bushel.
  - Soybeans: August WASDE reduced yields modestly but increased harvested area, with August pricing sustained by strong domestic crush margins and robust international demand; September WASDE again tightened ending stocks.
  - Wheat: Black Sea disruptions and port damage pressuring exports, combined with El Niño-related yield variability and Midwest drought, tightening global wheat supply; Chicago Soft Red Winter futures reflect this pressure.
  - Rough rice: prices at an 18-month high due to low domestic production and India’s monsoon-driven yield risk premiums.
- Forward look:
  - Oats and winter wheat have mostly harvested; corn and soybeans remain exposed to weather risk into the autumn. Weather volatility may remain a key driver through the winter, while geopolitical developments could continue to shape sentiment and risk premiums.
  - The market appears to be shifting from purely weather-driven concern to a broader macro risk environment, with stocks, demand resilience, and regional energy costs influencing price dynamics.

Bottom line: The near-term outlook for grains and oilseeds is shaped by tight supplies (especially corn and soybeans), ongoing geopolitical and weather uncertainties, and elevated input costs. Prices could remain elevated with continued volatility as winter harvests approach and supply/demand balances reassess.
